subjects.displayTitle: House of Worship: a gathering place for prayer and service
subjects.introduction: What might grow around a place where people of every background are welcomed to pray? These selections imagine a House of Worship whose influence extends into education, healing, hospitality, and the daily life of a community. The movement from silent listening to service is central to the Baha’i conception of the Mashriqu’l-Adhkar: devotion finds expression in institutions and relationships that nurture human oneness. The letters also bring this large vision close to the ground, through a small gift, a borrowed room, a caretaker’s labor, a committee’s decision, or a stone carried by hand. The connected subjects on sacred places, music, devotional gatherings, community building, and humanitarian activity invite us to ask how inward reverence becomes a shared way of life. These historical selections include directions for particular places and circumstances, as well as recorded conversations and later institutional explanations; their dates and authority matter when different practices or stages of development appear side by side. Isaiah’s welcome to those who fear exclusion, the Qur’an’s concern for threatened places of worship, and the prayerful sharing described in Acts offer distinct settings for exploring hospitality and collective responsibility. As the sequence unfolds, the building becomes an invitation to consider what people can create together when worship, beauty, consultation, and practical care inform one another.
subjects.arc: A door open to everyone → Prayer takes root in a community → The voice, the garden, and the form → A center of learning and care → Hands that build, hearts that give → Consultation becomes a shared undertaking → One beginning and many future houses → Wisdom amid difficulty → The promise carried forward → Further supplied readings: worship and service together

questions: What would make a House of Worship feel open to everyone? How do the passages connect the experience of entering and listening with the recognition of human oneness?
How do the descriptions of schools, medical care, shelter, and other services change your understanding of worship? What would a community learn by considering its neighbors’ needs?
What do the accounts of small gifts, humble caretakers, and people carrying stones reveal about the meaning of participation? How might these accounts reshape ideas of importance or recognition?
How do consultation, financial responsibility, perseverance, and discretion contribute to a shared undertaking? What do the dated local directions teach about reading guidance in context?

references.label: 1 · Isaiah 56:1–8 · A house of prayer for all peoples
references.note: Isaiah brings strangers and those who fear exclusion into a promise of welcome, joining worship with justice and covenant faithfulness. Read this beside the opening passages on a House of Worship open to everyone. What makes a place welcoming in practice? Attend to the Sabbath, covenant, and altar in Isaiah’s setting as you compare the two visions.
references.verified: Primary text read in the King James Version on Bible Gateway on 2026-10-10: all eight verses, including the ethical opening, the promises to eunuchs and foreigners, and the gathering of others.

references.label: 2 · Qur’an 22:39–41 · Protecting places of remembrance
references.note: These verses speak of people expelled for their faith and name monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques threatened with destruction. They place prayer alongside almsgiving and moral responsibility. Compare their concern for sacred places with the compilation’s passages on welcome, persecution, and wise action. How do the texts understand what a community owes to worshippers beyond its own circle? Keep in view the Qur’anic passage’s particular context of permission to resist aggression.
references.verified: Primary verses 22:39–41 read in the page’s context panel on Quran.com on 2026-10-10, in Dr. Mustafa Khattab’s The Clear Quran. The preceding permission to fight back and the following prayer and alms were read along with verse 40; the comparison does not equate different teachings about force.

references.label: 3 · Acts 2:42–47 · Prayer and shared provision
references.note: Acts portrays a community whose prayers, shared meals, teaching, and provision for need form a common life. Compare this account with the relationship between worship and service developed in the supplied institutional readings. What practices make inward devotion visible in care for others, and how do the forms of community life differ?
references.verified: Primary text read in the King James Version on Bible Gateway on 2026-10-10: Acts 2:42–47 in full. The comparison concerns communal practice, without treating the early Christian arrangement as identical to Baha’i institutions.
